slides: Before you practice, here's a quick summary of the topic. Reading a definition, the types, and the shortcuts.

slides.say: A new operation is just a definition. Read it, then follow the whole recipe. a heart b is three times a plus b, so four heart two is eighteen. And the order can matter, two star five isn't always five star two.
Whatever goes in, goes in brackets. Diamond of x is x squared minus five x, so diamond of negative two is four plus ten, fourteen.
Inside a longer exercise, turn each operation into a number first. Nested? Inside out, and don't stop halfway.
The operation works on an expression? Match the whole input first. F of four t is t plus three, so for F of twenty, t is five, and the answer is eight.
No definition? Put the input into each choice. An unknown input? Write the definition, and it's an equation.
Conditions? Check which rule at every step. Backwards? Try every rule, and keep an answer only if it fits.
Circular? Go down to the start value, then climb back up. On both sides? Isolate it like an unknown.

Not always? One example. Always? Swap the letters. Must be true? Plug in, but not zero, one or equal values, and try a second number if two survive. And a must-be-true question can eat your time, skip it and come back.
Two families undo themselves, c minus x and c over x. An inverse operation undoes the steps in reverse order.
A number minus its opposite? The even powers cancel, the odd ones double. And look for the shortcut formulas. [pause] That's it. Now go practice, and I'll see you in the next video.
